paras: Thank you for the half hour this morning. Here is a short recap, so that we are working from the same version. If anything below does not match what you remember, please correct me today rather than next month.

Decided. We will run a small pilot with two of your customers in the south of Brazil, on the standard integration, with no changes to the platform. You do not have to sign anything at this stage: a pilot of this size does not go through your procurement. The one thing that must happen before we start is the security questionnaire, because your legal team will not open a file without it.

Still open. The start date. You said you need to speak to your delivery team before you commit to anything in October, and that is fair. I have written it down as open rather than agreed, and I would rather have it open in writing than agreed in nobody's head. The second open point is who covers the first line of support during the pilot. Neither of us said it out loud, and it is the sort of thing that becomes a blocker in week three.

Action items. I will send the security questionnaire and a two-page description of the integration by Wednesday. Marta will confirm the technical contact on the Harbrook side by Friday. Both of us should read the other one's material before the next call, and I will circulate the notes from that call the same afternoon. If I have not heard back on the questionnaire, I will follow up next Tuesday, and if October turns out to be impossible, let us touch base in January anyway.

items: The partner has to sign a document before the pilot can start.
The email says 'You do not have to sign anything at this stage', which means it is not required, not that it is forbidden.
The security questionnaire is a condition for starting.
The email says 'The one thing that must happen before we start is the security questionnaire, because your legal team will not open a file without it'.
The start date was agreed during the call.
The email lists the start date under 'Still open' and says it is written down 'as open rather than agreed'.
Reading the other side's material before the next call is a requirement.
The email says 'Both of us should read the other one's material', which is a recommendation, not an obligation.
The writer has already decided when to chase the questionnaire.
The email says 'If I have not heard back on the questionnaire, I will follow up next Tuesday'.

items.situation: Their legal team will not start without the form. Say that in one sentence.
tips: The questionnaire must be returned before we can start.
Must, because the rule comes from outside the two of you.

items.situation: Signing is optional at this stage and you want to reassure them. Say it.
tips: You do not have to sign anything at this stage.
Not 'you must not sign' -- that would mean forbidden.

items.situation: You are recommending, not requiring. Say it about talking to their technical team.
tips: You should talk to your technical team before the demo.

items.situation: The partner will not commit to a date. Put that in the recap in two sentences.
tips: The start date is still open, because you need to speak to your team.
I will follow up next Tuesday.

items.situation: Somebody wrote: we will look into it. What is missing?
tips: A name and a date. Nobody is 'we'.
Without an owner it is a wish, not an action item.

items.situation: There is no news but you do not want the deal to go quiet. Say what you propose.
tips: Shall we touch base in two weeks, even if there is nothing new?
Touch base = brief contact, not a full meeting.

listenings.text: I write the recap within an hour, always, and I do it before I do anything else, because after an hour everybody has a slightly different meeting in their head, and the first thing that gets written down becomes the true one. It is not administration. It is the last move of the negotiation. There are three parts and I never skip any of them. What was decided. What was not decided. And the action items, with a name and a date on every single line. The middle one is the part everybody leaves out, and it is the part that saves the deal. If I write, the start date is still open because you need to speak to your team, then the open question is in front of somebody, and an open question in writing is a question that somebody will eventually answer. If I leave it out because it feels negative, it disappears, and in six weeks two companies are surprised at each other.

Most action items die for the same two reasons, and both of them are visible on the page. The first one is that nobody owns it. A task with no name on it is not a task, it is a wish, and everybody in the room quietly assumes somebody else will pick it up. The second one is that there is no date. If a line has no date, nothing about it can ever be late, and if nothing can be late, nobody is ever behind. That is why we will look into it is the most useless sentence in business English. Nobody is we, and look into it is not a verb anybody can be measured on. One more thing, and this is the one people find uncomfortable. If somebody refuses to take a deadline, write down that they refused, politely, and say when you will follow up. The refusal is information. It belongs in the recap exactly like everything else does.
